passage:
The train to Lucknow was three hours late, and rain roared on the platform roof. Madhav sat on a bench between his bag and a retired schoolteacher named Yusuf, who was doing a crossword. Across the tracks, a funeral procession passed under umbrellas.
"Why do people die?" Madhav asked suddenly, over the noise.
Yusuf put the pencil down. "That's a big question. Everything alive has a time. Some go early, some late, and nobody chooses it."
"But why are we here at all?"
"I don't know the whole answer," Yusuf said. "People have different ideas. Some say we're here to love and to learn. What do you think?"
Madhav watched the umbrellas. "Maybe to look after each other," he said. Yusuf nodded. "That's a good start."

qa.q: How late was the train to Lucknow?
qa.a: It was three hours late.

qa.q: What might Madhav be feeling when asking suddenly why people die, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Madhav is probably curious and a little uneasy. Asking out of the blue while a funeral procession passes suggests the thoughts had been building.

qa.q: What did Yusuf do that made his answer respectful of the question?
qa.a: Yusuf answered honestly, admitted not knowing everything, mentioned that people have different ideas and asked what Madhav thought.

qa.q: How might Yusuf have felt about being asked such a big question by Madhav?
qa.a: Yusuf probably took it seriously, since Yusuf put down the pencil and answered carefully, perhaps with a little tenderness.

grounding: A child asks why people die and why we are here; an honest, simple answer respects the questions.

passage:
Usha was supposed to be asleep, but her eyes were wide open under the blanket. "Mummy, why are we here?"
Her mother, Lavanya, switched on the small lamp. "Here in this room?"
"No. Here. On earth. And what happens to Dadu now that he's gone?"
Lavanya sat on the bed. The flat was quiet, except for the fridge humming. "I love that you ask this. I don't know all the answers, Usha. Some people believe Dadu is at peace, some believe he's part of everything around us. What I know is that we remember him, and he is still part of who we are."
Usha thought. "I remember his tea-stirring."
"So do I. Tell me more."
Usha curled up against her mother's arm and started to tell it.

qa.q: What did Usha remember about her grandfather?
qa.a: She remembered his tea-stirring.

qa.q: What was Usha probably feeling as she lay awake asking why we are here?
qa.a: Usha was curious and probably a little sad and unsettled about Dadu having gone. The wide-open eyes suggest she couldn't rest with the questions.

qa.q: What did Lavanya do that helped Usha feel her questions were welcome?
qa.a: Lavanya said she loved the questions, admitted she did not know all the answers and shared what she knew. She then invited Usha to say more about the memories.

qa.q: How might Lavanya have been feeling as she answered?
qa.a: Lavanya may have felt tender and a bit sad herself, since Dadu is gone. She stayed calm and honest and did not brush the questions off.

grounding: A child asks why we are here and what happens after death; honest, simple answers respect these early meaning-making questions.

passage:
After Nani died, I had a lot of questions. I asked Chandrika didi, my cousin, because she's in college and knows things.
"Why do people die?"
She didn't say "don't think about it." She said, "Bodies get old and tired, like Nani's did, and one day they stop working."
"Where did Nani go?"
"Different people believe different things. Some believe in heaven, some believe we come back. I'm not sure. I think she's in all the things she taught us."
"Why are we even here, then?"
Chandrika didi laughed a little. "Big question, Alka. I think maybe to love people and learn stuff."
I liked that she said "I'm not sure." It made me feel she was telling me the truth. That night I made Nani's lemon rice with Mummy.

qa.q: Who did Alka ask about why people die?
qa.a: Chandrika didi, Alka's cousin in college.

qa.q: Why did Alka like that Chandrika didi said 'I'm not sure'?
qa.a: It made Alka feel the answers were the truth, which seemed to comfort Alka more than a neat answer would have.

qa.q: How could a grown-up answer a child's big questions like these?
qa.a: Like Chandrika didi, they could give simple, honest answers, share different beliefs, and admit when they don't know.

qa.q: What would change if Chandrika didi had said 'don't think about it'?
qa.a: Alka might have felt confused and alone with the questions, and less able to grieve for Nani openly.

grounding: Shows a child asking why people die and why we are here, and being respected with simple honest answers instead of deflection.

passage:
Class 3 note, Thursday.
This morning we found Bubbles, our class fish, floating at the top of the tank. Most of the children were sad for a few minutes, then went back to drawing. Sumit (8) stayed by the tank. He asked me, "Why do things die? Will Bubbles be sad now? Where does a fish go?" Arnab, next to him, said, "Don't be silly, it's just a fish."
I didn't brush it off. I told Sumit that all living things have a life that ends, that Bubbles can't feel sad anymore, and that people believe different things about what happens after. He listened carefully and asked, "Will you die?" I said, "One day, when I'm very old, I hope."
We buried Bubbles in the garden at lunch. I've told his mother at pickup so she can continue the conversation at home.

qa.q: What was the class fish called?
qa.a: Bubbles.

qa.q: What does Sumit staying by the tank suggest about him?
qa.a: It suggests Sumit was curious and troubled, and wanted to understand death rather than move on like the others.

qa.q: What did the teacher do next that respected Sumit's questions?
qa.a: They answered simply and honestly instead of brushing it off, held a small burial, and told his mother so she could continue the talk at home.

qa.q: How does Arnab see Sumit's questions?
qa.a: Arnab thinks they are silly because to him it was 'just a fish'.

grounding: Shows a child asking why things die and what happens next, and a teacher answering honestly and simply.

passage:
Monday night, in bed with the torch.
Dear Diary, today I asked Ritu Masi the biggest question. We were shelling peas on the balcony and I said, "Masi, why are we here? Like, why are there people at all?"
She didn't laugh or say "eat your peas." She put the bowl down. She said, "Honestly, Bhavna, nobody knows for sure. Some people think God made us for a reason. Some think we just happened. I think we're here to look after each other and notice nice things, like these peas."
Then I asked what happens after we die. She said she doesn't know that either, and that people have wondered about it for thousands of years.
I felt kind of grown-up that she told me the truth. I'm going to keep asking her things.

qa.q: What were Bhavna and Ritu Masi doing on the balcony?
qa.a: They were shelling peas on the balcony.

qa.q: How did Bhavna feel when Ritu Masi answered honestly?
qa.a: Bhavna felt kind of grown-up and trusted, pleased to be told the truth instead of being brushed off.

qa.q: What did Ritu Masi's way of answering get right?
qa.a: She stopped what she was doing, gave simple honest views, and admitted what nobody knows, which respected Bhavna's big question.

qa.q: What would change if Ritu Masi had said 'eat your peas'?
qa.a: Bhavna might have felt silly for asking and stopped bringing big questions to Masi.

grounding: Shows a child asking why people exist and what happens after death, and an adult answering simply and honestly instead of deflecting.

passage: After old Hariram from the next lane was cremated, Charu sat on the edge of the village well, swinging her legs and watching the smoke thin out over the fields. Her cousin Trisha sat beside her. "Didi, why do people die?" "Bodies get very old or very sick, and then they stop working," Trisha said. "It happens to every living thing." Charu frowned. "Then why are we even here?" "I don't fully know. Some people say it's to love each other and do good work. What do you think?" "To look after the goats," Charu said seriously. "And what happens after?" "Families believe different things. Nobody knows for sure. Dadi believes he has gone to God." Charu nodded and held Trisha's hand all the way home.

qa.q: Where did Charu sit after the cremation?
qa.a: She sat on the edge of the village well, swinging her legs.

qa.q: What might Charu have been feeling when she asked why people die?
qa.a: She was probably curious and a little unsettled after the cremation, trying to make sense of death.

qa.q: What made Trisha's answers helpful?
qa.a: They were honest and simple, she admitted what she didn't know, and she asked what Charu thought instead of changing the subject.

qa.q: What would change if Trisha had said, "You're too small for such questions"?
qa.a: Charu might feel her questions were wrong and keep her worries to herself, instead of feeling close enough to hold Trisha's hand all the way home.

grounding: Shows a child asking why people die, why we are here and what comes next, and an older cousin answering honestly and simply.
